content: A robust framework for monitoring and evaluation is essential to enhance early cancer diagnosis services. Indicators should be collected at community, facility, and/or national levels, focusing on structural, input, process, or outcome measures. Key indicators for early diagnosis include the duration of patient, diagnostic, and treatment intervals, as well as the stage distribution at the time of diagnosis. Targets must be developed based on a valid and current situational analysis, prioritizing metrics relevant to the national and local context. Data should be analyzed by sex, geographic location, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status to identify and address inequalities in cancer care. Monitoring and evaluation systems are required at facility, community, and national levels. At health facilities, quality monitoring should assess delays in care, incomplete referrals, adherence to guidelines, and adverse event monitoring systems. Outcome monitoring should integrate continuous quality improvement by linking data to service delivery improvements and providing performance feedback to providers. Monitoring should extend beyond data entry to include serial audits to identify areas for care improvement. Data generated from assessments must guide decision-making for planners, managers, and providers by addressing identified deficits. Robust health information systems at the facility level can support the evaluation of integrated services by documenting patient status to identify delays or obstacles to care. This can be organized through hospital-based cancer registries aimed at improving care quality for individual patients, facility planning, and service delivery. At the community level, regular surveys of small patient samples (e.g., at least 100 patients per cancer type recruited from various facilities nationwide) can provide data on core process indicators, such as the duration of early diagnosis intervals. These surveys, conducted every five to six years, can assess progress and inform program planning. Cancer advocates and patients are valuable sources of feedback and can contribute to quality improvement through focus groups. Population-based cancer registries are critical at national and subnational levels for collecting cancer data and calculating incidence and mortality rates within defined geographic regions. Data are also necessary to track care accessibility and quality, referral timeliness, coordination between care levels, and resource allocation. Participation in and support of population-based cancer registries benefit not only the community but also national and international cancer control programs. Delays in cancer diagnosis and treatment access significantly contribute to global cancer morbidity and mortality. Solutions must focus on comprehensive health system responses and service integration, prioritizing high-impact and cost-effective interventions. Early diagnosis improves cancer outcomes by increasing the likelihood of successful treatment, reducing costs, and minimizing the complexity of interventions. The principles of early diagnosis are relevant across all resource levels and include increasing cancer awareness, promoting accurate clinical evaluation and staging, and improving access to care. These investments are particularly important in addressing disparities and ensuring access to cancer care for all. Cancer deaths have profound repercussions for families and communities. By implementing effective strategies for early cancer detection, lives can be saved, and the personal, societal, and economic burdens of cancer care can be reduced.
